questions.prompt: A basic feasible solution of \(Ax = b\), \(x \ge 0\), with \(A\) of full row rank, is obtained by
questions.explanation: The basis is an invertible block of columns. The nonbasic variables are set to zero, and the square system \(B x_B = b\) is solved. The result is feasible only when \(x_B \ge 0\). A negative basic variable is a basic solution and not a feasible one. Copying the right-hand side onto every variable ignores the columns. Zeroing the basic variables and solving for the others reverses the definition.

questions.figure_alt: A small array with two short rows of labels.
options: setting every variable equal to the matching right-hand side entry
choosing an invertible basis, setting the other variables to zero, and solving, provided the basic variables are nonnegative
choosing any invertible basis and accepting the solution even when a basic variable is negative
setting the basic variables to zero and solving for the nonbasic ones

questions.prompt: For \(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 6\) and \(x_1 + 2x_2 + x_4 = 10\), with all variables nonnegative, the basis of columns 1 and 2 gives basic variables \(x_1\) and \(x_2\). What is \(x_2\)?
questions.explanation: The basis matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), with determinant 1. Solving gives \(x_1 = 2\) and \(x_2 = 4\), and both are nonnegative, so the point \((2, 4, 0, 0)\) is feasible. Check: \(2 + 4 = 6\) and \(2 + 8 = 10\). Reporting 2 gives \(x_1\). Reporting 6 or 10 gives a right-hand side. Reporting 0 gives a nonbasic variable.

questions.prompt: For the same system, columns 1 and 3 produce \(x_1 = 10\) and \(x_3 = -4\). That basis is
questions.explanation: Independence makes the solution basic: the nonbasic variables are zero and the square system has one solution. Feasibility also needs every variable nonnegative. Here \(x_3 = -4\), so the point is not in the polyhedron. The equalities do hold; that is what the square solve enforces. Optimality is a statement about a cost, and this point is not even feasible.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
options: a basic feasible solution, because the columns are independent
optimal for every linear objective
infeasible as a point of the original system, because it ignores the equalities
a basic solution that is not feasible, because a basic variable is negative

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order used to build one basic feasible solution.
questions.explanation: A basis is a choice of independent columns, so the choice comes first. The square solve needs that basis. The nonbasic variables are then set to zero; doing that before the basis is chosen does not say which variables are nonbasic. Nonnegativity is the feasibility test, and it is applied to the solution just computed. Accepting a negative basic variable skips the last step and leaves the polyhedron.

steps: Choose as many independent columns as there are rows, and call that set the basis.
Solve the square system for the basic variables.
Set every variable outside the basis to zero.
Accept the point only when every basic variable is nonnegative.

questions.prompt: For \(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 6\) and \(x_1 + 2x_2 + x_4 = 10\), with \(x \ge 0\), which points are basic feasible solutions?
questions.explanation:
The feasible bases are columns \(\{1, 2\}\), \(\{1, 4\}\), \(\{2, 3\}\), and \(\{3, 4\}\), with points \((2, 4, 0, 0)\), \((6, 0, 0, 4)\), \((0, 5, 1, 0)\), and \((0, 0, 6, 10)\).
• \((10, 0, -4, 0)\) solves the equalities with columns 1 and 3, and \(x_3\) is negative.
• \((3, 3, 0, 1)\) satisfies both equalities and has three positive variables, so it is not a basic solution.

questions.prompt: A diagonal basis has entries \(a\) and \(d\), and the right-hand side is \((p, q)\), with every name positive. The sum of the two basic variables is
questions.explanation: The square system separates: the first basic variable is \(p/a\) and the second is \(q/d\). Their sum is \(p/a + q/d\). On the declared ranges both terms are positive, so the basis is feasible. Adding \(a\) and \(d\) in the numerator swaps the roles of data and basis entries. Using \(p/a + q/a\) reuses the first pivot for the second row.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a two-column array</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">b   n</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   0</text></svg>

questions.prompt: A note treats columns 2 and 4 of \(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 6\), \(x_1 + 2x_2 + x_4 = 10\) as a basic feasible solution. Exactly one step is false.
questions.explanation: Column 2 is \((1, 2)\) and column 4 is \((0, 1)\), so the matrix and its determinant are right. The solve gives \(x_2 = 6\) and \(x_4 = -2\), with the other variables zero. Invertibility is what makes the solution basic. Feasibility fails because \(x_4\) is negative. The last step treats independence as if it included the sign check.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
steps: Its determinant is 1, so the columns are independent.
Because the basis is invertible, this solution is a basic feasible solution.
reasons: \(x_4 = -2\), so the solution is basic and not feasible.
The determinant of that basis matrix is 0.

questions.prompt: For \(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 6\) and \(x_1 + 2x_2 + x_4 = 10\), the slack basis uses columns 3 and 4. What is the sum of the basic variables?
questions.explanation: Columns 3 and 4 are the identity, so the basic variables are the right-hand side itself: \(x_3 = 6\) and \(x_4 = 10\). Both are nonnegative. Their sum is 16. Reporting 6 or 10 reports one slack. Reporting 4 reports a basic variable from a different basis. The sum is a convenient check that both slacks were kept.

questions.prompt: A standard-form linear program that is feasible, and whose objective is bounded below, attains its optimal value
questions.explanation: The feasible set is a nonempty polyhedron with at least one extreme point, and a linear objective that is bounded below attains its minimum at an extreme point. Those extreme points are the basic feasible solutions. A strictly positive point is not needed, and an optimum on an edge can sit at a vertex of that edge. The relative interior is where a nonconstant linear function is never minimal. A basic solution with a negative entry is outside the feasible set, so it cannot be optimal.

options: at a basic feasible solution
only at a point where every variable is positive
only in the relative interior of the feasible set
at a basic solution that is allowed to have negative entries

questions.prompt: For \(x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 9\) and \(4x_1 + x_2 + x_4 = 12\), with \(x \ge 0\), the basis of columns 1 and 2 is feasible. What is the sum of its basic variables?
questions.explanation: The basis matrix is \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\). Solving gives \(x_1 = 1\) and \(x_2 = 8\), both nonnegative, and the slacks are zero. The sum is 9. Check: \(1 + 8 = 9\) and \(4 + 8 = 12\). Reporting 1 or 8 reports one coordinate. Reporting 12 reports a right-hand side. Reporting 21 adds a right-hand side to a coordinate.

questions.prompt: A basic feasible solution in which some basic variable equals zero is
questions.explanation: Nonnegativity allows zeros. A basic variable that lands on zero is still a feasible point, and the basis is called degenerate: more than one basis can describe it, and a later ratio test can take a step of length zero. The basis matrix was chosen invertible, and a zero in the solution does not change that determinant. Degeneracy does not by itself decide optimality.

options: infeasible, because a zero violates \(x \ge 0\)
not basic, because the basis matrix became singular
feasible, and called degenerate
the unique optimum of every linear objective

questions.prompt: The slack basis of \(Ax + s = b\), \(x \ge 0\), \(s \ge 0\), with the slacks as the basic variables, is a basic feasible solution when
questions.explanation: The slack columns form an identity basis, so the basic solution is \(s = b\) and \(x = 0\). It is feasible exactly when \(b \ge 0\). A negative entry of \(b\) makes that slack negative. The zero vector is the special case \(b = 0\), not the only feasible case. Free original variables would leave the standard form; the test here is only the sign of \(b\).
